text: Last lesson built a brand-new Gold table for the Regional Manager. Now it's time to close the loop and revisit the original one: gold.daily_sales_summary, built back in the Beginner project for the Store Operations stakeholder, before any of this incremental redesign existed. This chapter completely rewrote how Silver gets populated underneath it — so does this older table need to change too, or can it stay exactly as it was?

This table was never actually written to care how Silver gets populated in the first place. It only ever read Silver's current state and aggregated whatever was sitting there — group by store_id and sale_date, that's the whole job, nothing more. Silver went from a full nightly rewrite to an incremental MERGE INTO, but this table's responsibility never depended on which maintenance strategy Silver happened to be using underneath it at any given time.

Here's the aggregation again, unchanged: group silver.sales_clean by store_id and sale_date, sum total_amount into total_sales, count transaction_id into total_transactions, and overwrite the Gold table using mode overwrite, exactly like gold.category_breakdown. Compare it line by line against the Beginner project's original version — not one line of this actually changed.

That's the medallion pattern doing exactly its job: each layer depends on the contents of the layer beneath it, never on the process that produced those contents. As long as Silver's end state is correct, Gold's aggregation comes out correct automatically, with zero extra effort. And these totals are now actually more trustworthy than before, specifically because Silver itself got more trustworthy — that late-arriving sale from Lesson six now lands in the right day's total, instead of by pure luck.

Zoom out across this whole chapter for a second. Lessons five and six built a correct, late-data-safe MERGE INTO for Silver. Lesson seven built a brand-new category breakdown table for the Regional Manager. And this lesson confirmed the original daily summary table needed exactly zero changes. Both Gold tables now sit on top of one shared, correctly-maintained Silver layer.

That decoupling is exactly what let this team redesign the entire Bronze-to-Silver pipeline, a genuinely invasive change touching ingestion and the upsert logic both, without rippling anything into the Gold table downstream of it. Next lesson, you'll validate both Gold tables and prove, with real checks, that the numbers actually add up correctly.
